newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia rate fall depends on U.S, monetary growth.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia rate fall depends on U.S, monetary growth.

text.p: Malaysia's interest rates are forecast to fall next year, but the extent of the decline will depend on U.S. monetary policy and broad money supply growth in Malaysia, economists said on Thursday.
Domestic interest rates were expected to fall between 0.75 and 1.50 percentage points by the end of 1997, they said at a conference on interest rate futures.
Daniel Lian, regional economist with Natwest Markets in Singapore, said Bank Negara Malaysia's tight monetary policy had helped moderate monetary growth, but that was not enough.

"M3 (broad money supply) should be kept below 20 percent for a moderate period of time, say six to nine months, which we have not seen yet," Lian told the conference organised by the Malaysian Monetary Exchange.
And if the U.S. economy behaved as expected, there could be a 75-100 basis point drop in interest rates there, which could mean a similar decline in Malaysia.
"Our forecast is that interest rates will be trending downward, possibly by 150 basis points across all maturities," said Raja Lope Raja Shahrome, executive director of Rating Agency Malaysia Bhd.
He said his forecast was conditional on money supply expansion and inflation being kept under check, though a slowdown in economic growth suggested falling interest rates.
Malaysia expects to slow its gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 8.2 percent for 1996 from 9.5 percent in 1995, making it the ninth successive year of over eight percent growth.
A growing current account deficit and rising inflation had triggered worries about an overheating economy last year prompting the central bank to maintain a tight monetary policy.
The three-month interbank rate has risen by nearly 200 basis points in the last two years.
Earlier, in a Reuters poll, economists forecast a slower fall in Malaysian interest rates next year.

Economists from 10 research houses in Malaysia and Singapore forecast, on average, that the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) would be at 7.21 percent at the end of December this year, down from 7.33 on Thursday.
They forecast the three-month KLIBOR at an average 7.18 percent in March 1997 and at 7.03 percent by mid-1997.
The forecasts varied. Some economists expected Malaysia's tight monetary policy to ease next year due to slower economic growth and a shrinkage in the current account gap this year.

A majority of the economists polled said there might be a cut in interest rates towards the second half of 1997, if the mildly contractionary fiscal policy announced in the 1997 budget unveiled in October eases the burden on monetary policy.

"If growth slows down remarkably next year, then we may see the central bank lowering rates, conservatively, from the second quarter (of 1997) onwards," said Chung Tin Fah, general manager of O.S.K. Holdings Bhd.
But he added: "On the cautious side, they may maintain rates at the current level."

"If you look at the significant improvement managed on the trade front, and since interest rates tend to follow the current account deficit, there is scope for lowering rates next year," said Tan Min Lan, an economist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore.
Malaysia recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 163.2 million ringgit in the first nine months of 1996 against 8.2 billion in the corresponding period of last year.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
